newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: Protests dog EU efforts to set fur trap rules.
newsitem.headline: Protests dog EU efforts to set fur trap rules.

text.p: European Union environment ministers were met by an eight-metre (25-foot) high inflatable beaver on Tuesday as they met to discuss how to avert a trade row over a planned import ban on fur from animals caught in leg-hold traps.

Ministers heard a report from the European Commission on last week's talks in St Petersburg, Russia, with officials from Canada, the United States and Russia, the three main fur traders affected by the EU's proposed ban.

The report related to proposal COM(95)737 for a Council regulation amending Council Regulation (EEC) No 3254/91 prohibiting the use of leghold traps in the Community and on the import of pelts of animals which are caught using methods defined as inhumane by international rules.
"My impression after the meeting in St Petersburg is that there's been a certain amount of progress," EU Environment Commissioner Ritt Bjerregaard told a news conference.
"There's no doubt that environment ministers wish for a binding agreement," she said.

Beavers are among the thirteen animal species covered by the EU's proposed import ban, which had been due from the start of the year but which is on hold while the bloc negotiates less-cruel trapping standards with its partners.

Canada and the United States had threatened going to the World Trade Organisation in the event of the ban going ahead, mindful that nearly 70 percent of North America's $1.5 billion annual fur crop is exported to Europe.
Protesters from the Washington-based Animal Welfare Institute told reporters outside Tuesday's meeting that the EU risked back-tracking on its ban.
"They have developed a so-called standard which will still allow leg-hold traps to be used," said Wim de Kok, a consultant for the lobby group.
He added that proposed killing times of several minutes for traps would make animals suffer.

"We should apply the standards which we apply so carefully in slaughterhouses. If you think humane death for a farm animal should be a matter of seconds why should it be different for wild ones?" he said.

The main issues remaining for negotiators, according to one EU diplomat, are a U.S. request for a weaker legal framework for any deal, the question of the leg-hold trap ban itself, trap killing times for large animals and the species covered by new standards for several types of traps.
European negotiators are pushing for a four-year implementation period for the deal while Canada wants 10.
